_comment: The public roadmap, the single editable source for /roadmap. Locked with the founder on 2026-09-25 and checked against dpp-engine main (v0.14.0) and dpp-core main that day. Rules: features and outcomes only, written for a general reader. No issue links, commands, routes, crate names, version numbers or decision-record numbers; technical detail belongs on the docs site. No dates on anything that is not built. 'variants' lists the main forms a capability takes, in plain words. Update 'updated' whenever an item moves. 2026-09-30: eighteen items added with the founder, from a scan of the code, the planning documents and the standards landscape. 'Passports in the reader's language' and 'Product images' were folded into 'The finished public passport page'. The two 'Planned' items that wait on the per-node web address now say so in their own lines, because the register holds more than those two.

registers.title: Available now
registers.description: In the software today and exercised by its tests. Available is not the same as in use: nobody runs this in production yet.

items.title: Runs on your own infrastructure
items.line: One self-contained node on servers you choose. Build our setup tool once, and it sets up and starts the node. Self-hosting for your own compliance is free.

items.title: Signed with your own key
items.line: Every passport is signed on your servers, with a key that never leaves them, under an identity on a web domain you control. The key can be rotated without invalidating anything it already signed.

items.title: Releases that list their contents
items.line: Each release's container images carry a list of the components inside them and a record of how they were built, so you can check what you are running. The images are not public yet.

items.title: Spreadsheets in, passports out
items.line: Import your product data with a trial run first. The node reports what is wrong row by row instead of rejecting the whole file.

items.title: Checked before anything is signed
items.line: Each product group's rules run before signing, alongside warnings for values that look implausible. A new signed version of a group's rules can be installed on a running node without a restart.

items.title: Does it need a passport?
items.line: Ask the node whether a product group needs a passport, from when, and under which acts. Every date says whether it comes from the text of the law or from a reading of it.

items.title: Scan to read
items.line: The code on the product opens its public passport. No login and no fee.

items.title: The code, generated for you
items.line: The node generates each passport's QR code as an image, pointing to its public page.

items.title: Each reader sees what they are entitled to
items.line: Repairers, recyclers and authorities see more than the public, field by field, proven by a credential they hold rather than a setting they choose.

items.title: Export for industrial systems
items.line: Passports can also be served in the Asset Administration Shell format used by Industry 4.0 systems. The field meanings use Odal's own identifiers for now, so a receiving system still has to map them.

themes.theme: A record for the product's whole life

items.title: Changes without losing history
items.line: Correct a passport, replace it with a newer one, suspend it or retire it. Every earlier version stays readable, a code already printed on a product still works after its passport is replaced, and every change is written to a tamper-evident trail.

items.title: Passports keep working when the rules change
items.line: A new version of a product group's schema never breaks the passports issued under an older one. They keep resolving exactly as they were issued.

items.title: A handover between companies
items.line: Responsibility moves from one company to another on the record: the outgoing company signs the handover and the node signs its acceptance. Either side can decline or withdraw before it completes.

items.title: A second life, on the record
items.line: When a product is repurposed or remanufactured, its new passport links back to the passport, or passports, it came from, and says which of those happened.

items.title: Products made of products
items.line: A passport can point to the passports of its components, and the whole chain is verified in one check.

items.title: A recorded end of life
items.line: The end of a product's life is recorded on its passport, including the handover to a waste operator.

themes.theme: Proof that stands on its own

items.title: A proof file anyone can check offline
items.line: The passport, its signatures and its full history in one signed file. It verifies without a network connection and without trusting us.

link.label: Check a proof file in your browser

items.title: Readable when your server is not
items.line: A signed, pre-rendered copy of each public page can be kept outside the node, so a scan still works while the node is down.

items.title: A tamper-evident change log
items.line: Every change to a passport is logged. The log cannot be edited or deleted through the node, and each entry is chained to the one before it, so an entry altered behind the node's back shows.

items.title: One tool to run it all
items.line: Set up, onboard, import, publish, issue credentials and check status from a single tool.

items.title: Your systems stay informed
items.line: Passport events are sent to your own systems, signed so a receiver can tell a real delivery from a replayed one.

items.title: Scan counts you own
items.line: How often each passport was opened, counted on your own node. Nothing is recorded about the person who scanned.

items.title: Company details, recorded once
items.line: Your sites and company identifiers live on the node and are stamped onto every new passport.

items.title: The unsold-goods disclosure
items.line: Record what was discarded, why and where it went, line by line, ready for the yearly disclosure.

items.title: Clear about its own state
items.line: The node reports which of the services it relies on are fully working and which are still stand-ins, so it is clear what is not finished yet.

items.title: Safe by default
items.line: A node will not start with the sample passwords and keys from its own setup files. One set up for production also will not start while a service it relies on, such as sealing or rule checking, is only a stand-in. Overrides exist for development, and they are logged as warnings.

registers.title: Built, waiting on a legal step
registers.description: Finished and tested. What holds these back is not engineering: under eIDAS only a legal person can create an electronic seal, and there is no registered company behind the project yet.

items.title: Electronic seals with legal effect
items.line: Sealing works end to end today. Until a company holds a qualified certificate, every seal it makes says plainly that it carries no legal effect.

items.title: Registration in the EU registry
items.line: Registering passports needs the same legal identity. Our connection to the registry will be finished against its official interface.

registers.title: In progress
registers.description: Being built now. Nothing here is claimed as working.

items.title: More ways to identify a product
items.line: Every identifier scheme the European standard allows, not only a barcode number. The open library supports them now; the node does not use them yet.

items.title: Carbon and repairability figures in the passport
items.line: The node already checks a battery's declared recycled content against the legal minimums. The carbon and repairability calculators are written and published in the open library, but the node does not run them yet, so no passport carries a computed carbon or repairability figure today.

items.title: Spreadsheet import for every product group
items.line: Import covers most product groups today. Phones and tablets, and detergents, are still to come.

items.title: The unsold-goods report, ready to publish
items.line: The records exist today. What is missing is the finished document a company publishes on its own website each year.

items.title: Show only part of a passport
items.line: A passport can be issued as a digital credential its holder presents in part: they choose which fields to reveal, and the reader can still check those fields were signed. The open library has it; the node does not issue it yet.

items.title: A live passport you can scan
items.line: A sample passport served by a real node, which anyone can open from this website and scan with a phone.

registers.title: Planned
registers.description: Committed to, and not yet being built.

items.title: Proven against the standards
items.line: Each standard's own official tests, run against the software, with a plain statement of what passes. Alignment with all eight European standards for digital product passports, including the two on security.

items.title: Complete toy and detergent passports
items.line: Everything the toy and detergent regulations ask their passports to carry, which the software covers only in part today, including the local language and a colour image of the product.

items.title: The finished public passport page
items.line: The page a scan opens, in your company's look, in the reader's language, and with product images where the rules ask for them. Today's page is a plain placeholder.

items.title: Install without building anything
items.line: Ready-made images and a single install command, so a node runs without being built from source first.

items.title: JavaScript and TypeScript packages
items.line: Packages for building on a node in JavaScript and TypeScript, starting with a client for the node's interface. Each is built directly from the node's own interface and the open library, so it always says exactly what the node does. It waits on one decision first: how each node gets its own web address.

items.title: A dashboard for running your node
items.line: A web dashboard for the day-to-day work of running a node, built on those packages. It talks to your own node straight from your browser, so your data never passes through us. It waits on one decision first: how each node gets its own web address.

registers.title: Being considered
registers.description: Options, not promises. Not started, not scheduled, and deliberately without dates.

items.title: Keys in hardware you control
items.line: Signing keys held in a hardware security module or your own key service, rather than in an encrypted file on the server.

items.title: Proof on every scan
items.line: The public passport page checks the signature in the reader's own browser, so a scan shows that the passport was signed by its company and has not changed since.

items.title: A public checker anyone can run
items.line: Check any passport against the European standards on your own machine, without sending it anywhere.

items.title: Company identity through the European Business Wallet
items.line: The EU has proposed a wallet that lets a company prove who it is and sign and seal documents. It could give a company's passports their legal identity. It is a proposal, not law yet.

items.title: Readers identified by the EU Digital Identity Wallet
items.line: Repairers, recyclers and authorities prove who they are with the digital identity wallet every EU country is introducing, instead of a credential issued by the node.

items.title: Import any spreadsheet as it is
items.line: The node maps your own column names, number formats and material names, so you do not reshape your files to its template first.

items.title: Supplier data, signed at the source
items.line: Ask a supplier for component data, such as materials or recycled content, with a signed request, and receive a signed answer that goes straight into your passport.

items.title: The EU's shared vocabulary
items.line: Passport data expressed in the common vocabulary the EU maintains, so every system reads a field the same way.

items.title: Connected to industrial data spaces
items.line: Passports shared into industrial data spaces such as Catena-X, through the connectors those networks already use, rather than a network of our own.

items.title: Readable in the UN Transparency Protocol format
items.line: The same signed passport, also offered in the United Nations' format for supply-chain transparency, for trading partners who use it.

items.title: Rules that keep up with the law
items.line: A watch on the EU acts and standards that tells a node's operator what changed and which of their passports it affects.

items.title: Ready for the iron and steel passport
items.line: Iron and steel is expected to be the first product group to get a passport under the ecodesign rules. The software models it today and would follow the act as it is adopted.

items.title: Battery carbon footprint
items.line: Waiting on the EU to publish the calculation method. Guessing would produce a number that looks official and is not.

items.title: A practice copy of the EU registry
items.line: Somewhere to rehearse registering passports before connecting to the real registry.

items.title: Managed deployments
items.line: A node run for you, for companies that would rather not operate one themselves. It would still be yours alone: one company, one node, nothing shared with anyone else.

items.title: Update notices for self-hosted nodes
items.line: A signed channel that tells a self-hosted node when a new release is available.

items.title: Monitoring from your own tools
items.line: A node's health, workload and warnings, in the monitoring and alerting tools your company already runs.

items.title: A back-up copy held by an independent provider
items.line: A copy of each passport kept by an independent service provider, so it stays available even if the company that issued it, or its server, does not.

items.title: Records beyond passports
items.line: The node already signs a record about a company's year, the unsold-goods disclosure, not only about a product. The same approach could cover other reporting duties.
